articles.title: Federal probe of Ilhan Omar aimed at revoking citizenship, deporting her
articles.summary: Investigators are focused on her age when she became a citizen and have subpoenaed relatives, weeks before the Minnesota Democrat faces voters.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration's probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar is aimed at revoking her American citizenship and deporting her if investigators can prove that she or her relatives lied to immigration authorities when she became a citizen, according to two people familiar with the matter.

It would be an extraordinary step against a sitting member of Congress, and it is unfolding less than three weeks before Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, faces voters in an election she's likely to win easily.

On Oct. 12, agents from Homeland Security Investigations – the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement – searched Omar's Washington area home , carrying boxes of materials under a warrant tied to alleged immigration fraud and false statements. The Department of Justice has also subpoenaed some of her relatives , said one of the officials, who, like the other person, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the case.

The progressive congresswoman, a longtime political foe of President Donald Trump , has characterized the search as part of an intimidation effort meant to "target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."

"I will not be silenced," she wrote on social media earlier this week. Responding to the prospect, first laid out by the Wall Street Journal, of federal authorities working toward deporting the congresswoman, Omar's office said: "Trump's push to strip her of her citizenship and deport her has no basis in the law and has no precedent."

"This isn't a legitimate law enforcement action," Omar's top spokesperson, Jacklyn Rogers, said in a statement to USA TODAY. "It is an authoritarian move to silence an opponent right before an election where he and his party will be rejected by Americans in historic proportions."

The Trump administration has spent the past year reviving denaturalization, a legal tool once reserved mostly for war criminals and terrorism suspects. For decades, the government averaged about 11 such cases a year, according to an analysis from the Migration Policy Institute. Since Trump returned to office, the Justice Department has filed at least 163 cases and set a goal of 250 this month. But Omar, who was born in Somalia and came to the United States as a refugee in 1995, is by far the effort's most prominent target.

At the center of the case is a question about Omar's age. She became a citizen in 2000, at 17, through her father's naturalization, a route open only to children under 18. Investigators are trying to determine whether the family misstated her birth date so she would qualify, and whether her father, Nur Omar Mohamed, misrepresented his military history when he sought legal status.

The age question "seems to be the key focus now," one of the officials said.

Proving either would likely not be enough to deport her on its own. The government would first have to persuade a federal judge to revoke her citizenship, either in a civil case or through a criminal conviction, which triggers revocation automatically. Only then would she revert to her earlier immigration status and face possible removal. Her father, who would be central to any such case, died in 2020 from complications related to the coronavirus.

During an Oct. 13 interview with Fox News, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney in Washington, said that her office is separately investigating Omar's financial disclosures , adding that "if there was a crime that was committed it will be prosecuted."

Earlier this year, the bipartisan Office of Congressional Conduct, which reviews misconduct allegations against lawmakers, found no wrongdoing in Omar's filings , which had vastly overstated her wealth. Pirro said that finding "doesn't matter."

DHS targets Ilhan Omar’s residence. See photos of her political rise

Questions about Omar's background have followed her for most of her political career. A video that spread across conservative social media in 2019 claimed she had been 18, not 17, when her father applied. The theory resurfaced with reports that her staff, shortly after she arrived in Congress, asked Minnesota officials to change her birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982. Unfounded claims that she married her brother to help him immigrate to the U.S. have circulated for just as long.

Though the claims have been examined for years, by journalists and by her political opponents, no evidence has emerged to support any of them.

Still, over the past several months, officials at the highest levels of the Trump administration have embraced them publicly. In March, Vice President JD Vance declared, without evidence, that Omar "definitely committed immigration fraud," and said he and Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, had been discussing how the government might go after her. In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that if the government could prove she "shouldn't have been here in the first place," it would deport her.

For nearly as long as Trump has been in politics, Omar – a Somali-born refugee, Muslim and progressive whom he has often held up as a symbol of the immigration he wants to curb – has been one of his favorite foils. He has called Somali immigrants "garbage" and said Omar should be thrown out of the country.

Some of his allies have gone further. After the Oct. 12 search at Omar's home, Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina posted a call to "denaturalize and deport" her. That night, the audience at a Trump rally in Ohio chanted "deport" after he spoke about Omar and other Somali immigrants.

House Democratic leadership, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, called the search "deeply disturbing" in a joint statement.

"For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," they said. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family."

articles.title: Why the Katie Zacharia debacle is a huge embarrassment for Trump and his White House
articles.summary: In one fell swoop over the course of a week, the White House confirmed how rudderless, impulsive and hubristic its entire operation is — just ahead of the mi...
articles.body:
Katie Zacharia was on a media tour to save her job as White House press secretary on Friday when "Fox and Friends" host Lawrence Jones asked whether she wished she had disclosed never passing the bar exam, despite repeatedly claiming to be a lawyer .

Zacharia's response: "Those questions weren't asked."

And therein lies the problem: It's not a matter of qualifications — it's a basic question about her background that President Donald Trump and his White House failed to vet.

Zacharia's stunningly short and turbulent tenure as press secretary is far from the biggest or most substantial foul-up of Trump's second term. But it does rank remarkably high on the embarrassment quotient.

In one fell swoop over the course of a week, the White House confirmed how rudderless, impulsive and hubristic its entire operation is — and with just a few weeks to go before voters render their judgment on it in the 2026 midterm elections.

Trump fired Zacharia as press secretary on Friday, advisers told CNN, just five days after she started the job. Her tenure has set the new benchmark for brevity as a top Trump White House aide, halving the record set by first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci. ("A Scaramucci" has since become an informal unit measuring 11 days.)

Given that Trump personally selected Zacharia and he is generally loath to admit he's made a mistake, it took a pretty rough week to prompt her ouster.

In her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, Zacharia spent most of a 14-minute appearance nervously reading from a script that she repeatedly stumbled over before calling on just three reporters from conservative-friendly outlets.

Then she went on a stream of media appearances that only reinforced she would likely be a liability at the White House lectern. Trump subsequently pulled the plug without even giving her a second briefing.

It's embarrassing for a number of reasons.

It's not as if Zacharia was the product of a process that needed to be rushed; former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced her departure more than two months ago, on August 12 . That's plenty of time to make sure you have the right person.

The White House did have a series of candidates, CNN has reported , but some of them suffered from the unforgivable deficit of having occasionally said negative things about Trump. Zacharia's name emerged suddenly late in the process, after not being previously considered. And as with so many things, it appears those around Trump quickly turned his whim into reality.

There are understandable reasons for why Trump might have thought she could do the job, of course. He had undoubtedly seen her defending him on cable news plenty of times, his preferred method for screening job candidates. But serving as press secretary isn't the same as doing TV hits with often-friendly hosts. And her briefing performance was objectively brutal.

Then the White House compounded its mess.

It dispatched Zacharia on a media tour of friendly outlets, apparently in hopes of rallying support and showing she was up to the task. But it proved the opposite.

She was peppered with tough questions from conservative Trump allies who were ostensibly worried about her ability to handle being the face of the White House's messaging. And those appearances — more than the briefing — made Trump conclude that she "wasn't ready for prime time," a person with direct knowledge of his comments told CNN.

One of those skeptical conservative Trump allies was Fox News' Sean Hannity. On Tuesday night, he was reading from the typical playbook: bashing the "abusively biased, corrupt news media" for being mean to Zacharia. But during his interview with her Thursday night, he asked her a series of sober and probing questions.

Trump on Friday bemoaned how Zacharia was "made to suffer like she's suffered at the hands of the press." But it's a lot harder to make that argument when your own media allies have done the scrutinizing. (Some of them also dinged Zacharia for her resume inflation .)

And similar to Hannity, the White House now has egg on its face after initially vouching for Zacharia.

White House communications director Steven Cheung assured in an excitable social media post Tuesday morning that Zacharia had a "tremendous start" in which she "commanded the room." A White House press release hailed her "commanding" performance and clipped what it cast as her highlights. Later in the week, Cheung insisted she would be remembered as "one of the all-time greats" by the end of Trump's second term.

But perhaps the worst part of this whole episode for the White House is that it further solidifies a pre-existing narrative of Trump's chaotic leadership style and inability to effectively manage the federal government.

There's been plenty of grist for that mill, including Trump's recently aborted decisions to run taxpayer-funded political ads and to live stream an execution — both of which 80%-plus Americans opposed .

Earlier in his presidency, Trump rained chaos on the government by giving Elon Musk apparent carte blanche to do, seemingly, more or less whatever he wanted. Many people who were fired later had to be reinstated when it was discovered that, actually, they did really important jobs — or couldn't legally be fired.

There was Signalgate and the whiplash over Trump's tariffs and the administration's inability to get its story straight on the Iran war .

Similar to Zacharia, Trump also removed officials shortly after the Senate confirmed them, including the head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and his IRS commissioner. (In the latter case, he also removed the acting replacement after less than a week .) His first national security adviser was moved to another job after less than three months, thanks to Signalgate.

And the American people appear to have noticed. A CNN poll in July showed they disapproved of Trump's management of the federal government, 65%-35%.

Fully 74% of independents and even 28% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents disapproved.

"A Zacharia" doesn't have the same ring to it as "a Scaramucci" does. But her tenure is an unforced error that gives voters a similar shorthand at a remarkably inopportune time for Trump.

articles.title: Trump administration seeks to remove judge in golf course case, accusing her of ‘egregious’ behavior
articles.summary: The Trump administration has requested the removal of the federal judge overseeing a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul a Washingt...
articles.body:
The Trump administration has requested the removal of the federal judge overseeing a legal challenge to President Donald Trump's plans to overhaul a Washington, DC public golf course, accusing her of having "bias."

In a motion filed Friday, the administration's lawyer said US District Judge Ana Reyes' "behavior in this case is nothing short of egregious," pointing to a tense hearing earlier this week.

CNN previously reported that during Monday's hearing, Reyes — who was appointed to the bench by former President Joe Biden — said she was "furious" with the Trump administration for cutting down 169 trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without first notifying the court, adding that "the government can't be trusted."

In Friday's filing, the Justice Department lawyer said, "Judge Reyes's conduct rises to the level of deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy toward the Trump Administration," raising comments she made when overseeing other cases involving the administration.

"The Trump Administration is entitled to a neutral forum and an adjudicator who is capable of maintaining the appearance of impartiality," the lawyer continued. "Judge Reyes has demonstrated she cannot do that."

Friday's filing is part of a legal challenge from a preservationist group and two local golfers against Trump's plans to transform the East Potomac Golf Course into a championship caliber course. The proposed renovation is among several construction projects that the president has launched since returning to the White House as part of his efforts to reshape Washington, DC's physical landscape.

Federal officials said in a recent court filing that nearly 730 trees will need to be cleared as part of the renovation plan, describing it as routine maintenance meant to eliminate potential hazards.

The administration's lawyer also took issue with Reyes requiring "high-level" officials to be at the Monday hearing, writing that she "demonstrates a cavalier disregard for these officials' valuable time, as well as a blatant disregard for black-letter separation of powers principles she should be aware of as a federal judge."

The lawyer went on to point to comments that Reyes previously made when overseeing other cases involving the Trump administration to argue that there is a "pattern of animus."

According to the filing, Reyes said the administration is "literally erasing transgender people" with its ban on transgender service members. The judge ultimately blocked the ban.

articles.title: Idosa é amarrada, amordaçada e agredida durante tentativa de roubo | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítima foi encontrada por policiais militares em um dos quartos da residência, com ferimentos no rosto e sangue pelo chão. Um homem de 43 anos foi preso em flagrante em Presidente Prudente (SP).
articles.summary: Uma mulher de 84 anos foi encontrada amarrada, amordaçada e com ferimentos no rosto após ser agredida durante uma tentativa de roubo dentro da própria casa, em Presidente Prudente.
articles.body:
Polícia Civil também solicitou à Justiça a conversão da prisão em flagrante em preventiva — Foto: Polícia Civil/Divulgação

Uma mulher de 84 anos foi encontrada amarrada, amordaçada e com ferimentos no rosto após ser agredida durante uma tentativa de roubo dentro da própria casa, na Rua Major Felício Tarabay, na Vila Nova, na manhã deste domingo (18), em Presidente Prudente (SP). Um homem de 43 anos foi preso suspeito do crime.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, a vítima contou à Polícia Civil que se preparava para ir à feira e varria a garagem quando percebeu um homem atrás dela. Ao questioná-lo sobre o que fazia no local, ouviu que se tratava de um assalto e que não seria morta caso colaborasse.

De acordo com o relato, o suspeito exigiu dinheiro e empurrou a idosa para dentro da casa. Mesmo após ela dizer que não guardava dinheiro no imóvel, ele continuou a agredi-la com socos, puxões de cabelo e golpes que fizeram sua cabeça bater contra o chão. O homem também colocou um pano na boca da vítima e tentou amarrá-la.

Ainda conforme o boletim, o suspeito pegou uma faca na cozinha e tentou atingir o olho da mulher. Ela se defendeu com as mãos e machucou os dedos ao tentar se soltar das amarras.

A idosa relatou ter permanecido sob agressões por cerca de três horas , período em que chegou a desmaiar e recuperar a consciência diversas vezes. Segundo ela, o homem a ameaçava de morte e dizia que já havia matado outras pessoas.

A Polícia Militar chegou ao endereço depois de ser alertada por um homem que se identificou como policial e afirmou ter visto, por câmeras, um indivíduo pulando o muro da residência vizinha. Ele disse não ter visto o suspeito sair do imóvel.

Ao verificar a casa, os policiais encontraram um portão interno aberto e entraram na residência. Nos fundos, viram um homem sem camiseta observando a equipe. Ao perceber a aproximação dos policiais, ele fechou uma porta.

Após a porta ser aberta, o suspeito afirmou que havia entrado para furtar ou roubar e que iria se entregar. Segundo o boletim, ele resistiu à abordagem e precisou ser contido pelos policiais.

A equipe encontrou a idosa amarrada e amordaçada em um dos quartos, com ferimentos no rosto e sangue pelo chão. Depois de ser libertada, ela foi encaminhada para atendimento médico na UPA do Jardim Guanabara. A ficha médica apontou escoriações e hematomas na face.

O homem permaneceu em silêncio ao ser interrogado. Ele foi preso em flagrante por tentativa de roubo com restrição de liberdade da vítima. A Polícia Civil também solicitou à Justiça a conversão da prisão em flagrante em preventiva.

articles.title: Carreata reúne apoiadores de Lula em Juiz de Fora; VÍDEO | G1
articles.standfirst: Veículos saíram do bairro Cruzeiro do Sul, passaram pela Zona Norte e chegaram no estacionamento do Estádio Municipal. Segundo turno será no próximo domingo (25).
articles.summary: Veículos saíram do bairro Cruzeiro do Sul, passaram pela Zona Norte e chegaram no estacionamento do Estádio Municipal. Segundo turno será no próximo domingo (25).
articles.body:
Apoiadores do presidente Lula , candidato à reeleição pelo Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), reuniram-se neste domingo (18) para uma carreata pelas principais ruas de Juiz de Fora . A concentração aconteceu na Avenida Presidente João Goulart, no bairro Cruzeiro do Sul.

Com bandeiras, adesivos e camisas de apoio ao candidato, os participantes foram até a Zona Norte, passando pelos bairros de Benfica e Santa Cruz, e concluíram o ato no estacionamento do Estádio Municipal, já na Cidade Alta.

Também durante a manhã, eleitores bolsonaristas se reuniram na Praça Jarbas de Lery Santos, no bairro São Mateus, para uma mobilização em apoio ao candidato Flávio Bolsonaro.

Carreata em apoio ao presidente Lula, em Juiz de Fora — Foto: Juliana Netto/g1

O segundo turno para escolha do novo presidente será no próximo domingo (25). Ao todo, 395.457 eleitores estão aptos a votar.

No primeiro turno, Lula foi o candidato a presidente mais votado em Juiz de Fora, com 151.552 votos. Já Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 126.964 votos.

articles.title: Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro: as estratégias na reta final do 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Em cenário de empate técnico nas pesquisas, campanhas concentram agendas na região Sudeste na última semana antes da votação do dia 25 outubro e planejam explorar nas redes sociais os confrontos entre os candidatos nos debates.
articles.summary: Com empate técnico nas pesquisas, Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro focam no Sudeste e usam debates para conquistar eleitores na reta final do segundo turno.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e Lula (PT) em atos de campanha. — Foto: Reuters

Na última semana antes do segundo turno da eleição, marcado para o próximo domingo (25), as campanhas de Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) apostam nos debates e na mobilização nas ruas, principalmente nos estados do Sudeste, que concentram os maiores colégios eleitorais do país, para conquistar votos na reta final da disputa.

Enquanto o petista pretende explorar medidas de apelo popular para tentar reverter a vantagem de Flávio, que recebeu mais votos no primeiro turno, o senador prepara uma ofensiva para rebater os ataques do adversário e intensificar a divulgação de suas propostas e reforçar que manterá programas sociais .

A pesquisa Datafolha divulgada na quinta-feira (15) mostrou Flávio com 47% das intenções de voto e Lula com 45%, em situação de empate técnico. O levantamento da Quaest , divulgado na quarta-feira (14), também apontou empate técnico: 46% para o candidato do PL e 44% para o presidente.

Diante desse cenário, a campanha de Lula avalia que há espaço para uma virada. Já os aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro, embora confiantes na vitória, reconhecem a necessidade de intensificar a mobilização para assegurar a vantagem.

Flávio Bolsonaro prepara respostas e divulgação de propostas

O candidato à presidência do Brasil, Flávio Bolsonaro, do Partido Liberal (PL), faz campanha no bairro do Sarandí, uma das áreas mais atingidas pelas enchentes históricas de 2024, em Porto Alegre, Brasil, em 14 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Diego Vara

Na campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro, integrantes da equipe ouvidos pelo g1 afirmam que o senador pretende intensificar as respostas aos ataques de Lula e explorar nas redes sociais trechos dos debates entre os dois candidatos previstos para a reta final da disputa. O último será realizado pela TV Globo, na sexta-feira (23).

Nos últimos dias, parte da propaganda eleitoral e das publicações do senador se concentrou em rebater acusações de que, se eleito, cortará benefícios sociais. Agora, os aliados querem reforçar a divulgação de respostas a informações que classificam como falsas e, ao mesmo tempo, dar mais espaço às propostas do candidato.

O plano de governo do senador não prevê cortes em programas sociais. A campanha de Lula, porém, associa esse risco às declarações de Flávio em defesa da redução dos gastos do Estado.

Na avaliação da campanha, uma abordagem mais propositiva pode ajudar o candidato do PL a conquistar eleitores menos ideológicos, uma vez que os apoiadores mais alinhados à candidatura já estariam mobilizados.

Fim da escala 6x1 pressiona campanha do senador

Uma das principais apostas de Lula na reta final da disputa também se tornou um ponto de atenção para a campanha de Flávio: o fim da escala 6x1, promulgada pelo Congresso na sexta-feira (16) após aprovação no Senado.

Depois de terminar o primeiro turno com cerca de 2,2 milhões de votos a menos que Flávio Bolsonaro (uma diferença de 1,87 ponto percentual), o presidente atuou para acelerar a aprovação da proposta, que tem o apoio de 61% dos brasileiros , segundo pesquisa Quaest divulgada nesta semana.

Na avaliação de interlocutores das duas campanhas, a discussão tem potencial para mudar votos e ampliou o espaço dedicado às propostas dos candidatos.

Flávio Bolsonaro, que criticava a iniciativa, mudou de posição e votou a favor. A campanha de Lula passou, então, a explorar essa mudança para acusar o adversário de oportunismo.

Na reta final, a campanha de Flávio também pretende reforçar a mobilização nas ruas, com atos em cidades consideradas estratégicas e planeja participar no sábado (24) de um ato em Belo Horizonte organizado por Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG), deputado reeleito com recorde de votos. Depois, seguirá para o Rio de Janeiro.

Neste domingo (18), o senador também estará ao lado de Nikolas na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo. O ato é visto pela oposição como uma resposta à manifestação realizada no mesmo local, em apoio a Lula, na semana passada .

A campanha também avalia promover atividades em cidades do Nordeste, região onde os aliados de Lula buscam reduzir a vantagem do presidente.

Lula aposta em debates e mobilização nas ruas

O presidente brasileiro Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) à reeleição, gesticula durante um comício de campanha antes do segundo turno das eleições, em Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais, Brasil, em 16 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Pilar Olivares

Integrantes do PT ouvidos pelo g1 resumem a estratégia de Lula para a reta final do segundo turno em duas frentes: “debate e rua”.

A campanha do PT deve manter o ritmo de mobilização, e o presidente pretende manter a agenda de viagens pelo país, com prioridade para o Sudeste. Para encerrar a campanha, o partido anunciou um ato na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo, no sábado (24), véspera da votação.

Nos debates, a aposta é destacar medidas de apelo popular, como a proposta de tarifa zero no transporte público aos fins de semana, o fim da escala 6x1 e o projeto que amplia o limite de faturamento dos microempreendedores individuais (MEIs) e prevê o perdão de dívidas da categoria. Lula também prometeu criar um programa Pé-de-Meia para universitários caso seja reeleito.

Na avaliação de aliados, a campanha do presidente conseguiu assumir a iniciativa no debate político. Eles apontam como fatores positivos o desempenho nas redes sociais, o apoio de artistas e as mudanças na coordenação da campanha. Também consideram favorável a perda de espaço de temas como o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e o caso Banco Master na discussão pública.

“Isso aí não mexe com a vida do povo”, afirmou Jilmar Tatto, secretário nacional de Comunicação do PT, em referência a esses assuntos. “Enquanto o outro lado fica montando os gabinetes e os ministérios, a gente está na rua fazendo campanha.”

A campanha do segundo turno também foi marcada por uma ofensiva nas redes sociais. Lula passou a gravar vídeos em formato de selfie e reuniu jovens influenciadores eleitos, como Ana Eliza (PT-MG), Guilherme Cortez (PSOL-SP) e Ana Júlia Ribeiro (PT-PR), para ampliar sua presença nas plataformas digitais.

Outra mudança foi a entrada de lideranças petistas do Nordeste no comando da campanha. O senador Camilo Santana (PT-CE), ex-ministro da Educação e ex-governador do Ceará, assumiu a coordenação política. articles.title: Carro bate de frente com outro ao e deixa cinco feridos na SP-425 | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente foi registrado na manhã deste domingo (18), na Rodovia Assis Chateaubriand (SP-425), em Martinópolis (SP).
articles.summary: Uma colisão frontal entre dois carros deixou cinco pessoas feridas na manhã deste domingo (18), na Rodovia Assis Chateaubriand (SP-425), em Martinópolis (SP).
articles.body:
Batida frontal foi registrada na SP-425, em Martinópolis (SP), neste domingo (18) — Foto: Artesp/Reprodução

Uma colisão frontal entre dois carros deixou cinco pessoas feridas na manhã deste domingo (18), na Rodovia Assis Chateaubriand (SP-425), em Martinópolis (SP).

Segundo a concessionária Eixo SP, o acidente aconteceu na altura do km 407. Um dos automóveis seguia no sentido norte e, ao tentar ultrapassar um caminhão, não conseguiu concluir a manobra e bateu de frente com outro veículo, que trafegava no sentido contrário.

Inicialmente, as cinco vítimas foram classificadas em estado grave. Posteriormente, três delas tiveram o quadro reclassificado para moderado.

De acordo com a atualização mais recente, feita às 10h36, os ocupantes de ambos os veículos foram levados para atendimento médico.

Durante o atendimento da ocorrência, a rodovia ficou totalmente interditada nos dois sentidos. Os veículos foram retirados das faixas de rolamento e deslocados para o acostamento no aguardo da perícia, o que gerou um congestionamento de cerca de um quilômetro em cada sentido.

Até o momento, não há novas informações sobre o estado de saúde das vítimas.

articles.title: Meet the small DOJ unit approving some of Trump’s most controversial policies
articles.summary: When White House officials wanted to know if President Donald Trump could send the U.S. military to help capture President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a spe...
articles.body:
Meet the small DOJ unit approving some of Trump’s most controversial policies

When White House officials wanted to know if President Donald Trump could send the U.S. military to help capture President Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a special unit in the Justice Department assured them it was legal.

When the administration was preparing to strike suspected drug traffickers' boats on the open sea without congressional approval, the same small unit declared the action permissible.

When the White House asked if the Presidential Records Act was constitutional, the office ruled it was not, giving Trump the apparent green light to save fewer records from his second term.

As the Trump administration pushes the bounds of executive power, the Justice Department unit known as the Office of Legal Counsel, or OLC, has affirmed some of its most high-profile and controversial actions - even as many experts question their legitimacy and some are later struck down by the courts.

Tucked away on the Justice Department's fifth floor, the two dozen or so lawyers at the OLC are charged with assessing the legality of actions the executive branch wants to take, especially those that are novel or likely to be contentious. Much of its work, particularly on national security matters, remains shielded from public view, but some of the office's conclusions have emerged in often dense legal opinions.

The OLC during Trump's second term is not the first to be accused of adopting shaky reasoning to justify a president's policies. Under President Barack Obama, the OLC wrote a controversial rationale for launching a deadly drone attack on a U.S. citizen overseas. Under President George W. Bush, the office justified the used of "enhanced interrogation" - what some call torture - against enemy combatants, including waterboarding.

But because Trump has advanced so many controversial policies - including imposing global tariffs, refusing to spend congressionally allocated funds and pushing to more broadly deploy the National Guard - the OLC now faces particular scrutiny.

Critics contend that during Trump's second term, the OLC is sometimes responding to legal questions that appear personal to Trump, rather than addressing live policy debates, as is typical. For instance, Trump had quibbled over the Presidential Records Act after he was indicted in Florida for allegedly mishandling classified materials. These critics said the OLC opinion on this act seemed aimed at Trump's prior issues with the law, rather than any active policy issues.

"It is not inconsistent with the type of advice OLC of any flavor, Democrats or Republicans, would give to other presidents," said Carlos Uriarte, a Justice Department political appointee during the Biden administration who worked closely with the OLC. "What's different is that this administration seems to be more willing to go into theoretical questions that are not before them."

Trump's OLC is headed by T. Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old former solicitor general of Ohio described by current and former colleagues as a constitutional originalist who, like Trump, has an expansive view of executive power.

Gaiser, who represented Trump's losing presidential campaign in 2020 and refuses to acknowledge Joe Biden won that election, said his role in the Justice Department is to provide honest legal advice, not push for any particular outcome.

"We're the least interested in advocating, [and] the most interested in saying, 'Here's our frank view of where we think we stand in respect to the law,'" Gaiser told The Washington Post in a rare interview.

His sparsely decorated office is filled with bound books of legal opinions, which surround a desk Gaiser proudly says is believed to have once been used by former Supreme Court justice Antonin Scalia, who headed the OLC under President Gerald Ford.

People who know and have worked with Gaiser spoke positively about him, with former associates describing him as "brilliant." Gaiser clerked on the Supreme Court for Samuel A. Alito Jr. when the justice wrote the landmark opinion restricting abortion access. As OLC head, Gaiser has written conservative opinions backing restrictions around abortion access, expanded gun access and greater White House authority.

Gaiser said he has not hesitated to tell the White House when its ideas should not be enacted, though he declined to share specifics. Gaiser, and others familiar with the office, noted that the president is not required to listen to the OLC.

Much of OLC advice is shared privately. As a result, public perceptions of the OLC are largely shaped by the opinions it releases, even as they represent only a portion of its work.

The office's role could become even more central if Democrats take control of Congress. The office recently approved an expanded view of executive privilege, for example, which Democrats fear will be used to shield Trump's associates from testifying before Congress.

Gaiser's office could also get asked to provide legal advice if outcomes are challenged during and after next month's midterms. The office has already determined that the executive branch can legally seek a state's voter rolls and share them with immigration authorities - a key part of the Trump administration's strategy to identify noncitizen voters as it tries to argue that voter fraud is rampant.

Asked during the interview in his office who won the 2020 election, Gaiser demurred, citing his work as a lawyer for Trump's campaign that year.

He cannot say publicly who won, Gaiser said, because that would reveal too much about the privileged legal advice he gave Trump campaign officials when he was their attorney.

"Joe Biden was sworn in as the president. He was certified the winner of the election by the Congress," Gaiser said. "What I privately think happened in the 2020 election - what advice I provided to the president as the head of the campaign or to others in the campaign, the other campaign lawyers - that's the kind of stuff I just really can't get into ."

Although many Trump appointees display sharp elbows and make frequent appearances on cable news shows, Gaiser takes a lower profile, even as his work is attracting increased attention, including from Democratic lawmakers and federal courts.

After the OLC declared in April that the Presidential Records Act was unconstitutional, a federal court responded to lawsuits and said that, at least for now, the White House had to preserve records as normal. Advocacy groups are fighting to unseal the OLC's memo justifying the deadly boat strikes in international waters.

One former OLC attorney, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer a sensitive assessment, said the office's opinions are based on shoddy legal arguments.

Under previous administrations, "you have opinions that at least try to grapple with counterarguments," but that is not the case today, the former OLC lawyer said.

Gaiser sharply disputes the assertion that his office's opinions are not high-quality, saying he and his lawyers deliver honest, accurate assessments.

"There is a continuum with the advice you give. You can say, this is lawful but risky. This is lawfully safe. This is unlawful," Gaiser said. "OLC has a measure of independent counsel that we offer."

During the first Trump administration, the OLC pushed back on some of the president's most explosive actions. Steve Engel, then head of the OLC, testified about the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol that he had advised Trump appointees that some of their plans to question the results of the 2020 presidential election were not legal.

Under Engel, the OLC also advised that an executive order ending birthright citizenship - the legal principal that virtually everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen - would be unconstitutional, according to multiple people familiar with the matter, and the president did not issue one.

But when Trump became president a second time, he issued an order to end birthright citizenship on his first day in office. The OLC did not review it or the other executive orders Trump issued immediately upon his return, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The Supreme Court later affirmed birthright citizenship in a ruling that Trump called a "miscarriage of justice."

Gaiser, who was confirmed in July 2025, had not taken office at that point, and said his office has since reviewed all of the president's executive orders before they are issued.

The OLC attracted a burst of attention in August when it issued an opinion on executive privilege, which can shield communications between presidents and their aides. The office declared that the doctrine covers not only official advisers, but can also expand to cover outside associates consulted by the president in certain circumstances.

The opinion was released as the American Bar Association was suing the Trump administration over its efforts to sanction law firms that hired Trump's perceived foes or took on cases he disliked. The ABA is seeking testimony from Boris Epshteyn, one of Trump's outside advisers.

The ABA assailed the OLC opinion as self-serving and suspiciously timed. But Michael Edney, who worked at the OLC under Bush, said the opinion's reading of executive privilege was not unreasonable, given the importance that some presidents place on outside consultation.

"It's not all that crazy to me," he said.

Most experts said that while OLC lawyers are not required to be blind to the president's agenda, they cannot simply interpret the law to suit his priorities. Former OLC employees said the office should not be a rubber stamp, regardless of whether the president heeds its opinions.

"In the executive branch, like everywhere else in the world, lawyers give advice and clients make decisions," Edney said. "Their job is to provide legal advice."

articles.title: House panel warns Singham-linked nonprofits: Comply with subpoenas or face Congress
articles.summary: Neville Roy Singham and 20 others face potential depositions as the House Ways and Means Committee escalates its probe into nonprofit foreign funding.
articles.body: Lawmakers have escalated their probe of three nonprofits linked to Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham's funding network, warning that their leaders — and even Singham himself — could be hauled before Congress to answer questions under oath unless they comply with subpoenas by Tuesday. In new letters announced this week, the Republican-led House Ways and Means Committee renewed its demands for financial records and other documents as lawmakers investigate whether millions of dollars flowing through Singham's network of tax-exempt nonprofits are being used to advance Chinese Communist Party interests in the United States. Singham himself is among 21 individuals identified by the committee for potential questioning under oath, according to Fox News Digital sources. The list includes nonprofit executives, activists and journalists associated with the three organizations. PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS The letters were sent to The People's Forum Inc., a New York City-based activist hub; BreakThrough News, a left-wing nonprofit media outlet that shares a Manhattan address with The People's Forum; and Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, a Massachusetts-based Marxist think tank. "Shanghai Singham has poured millions of dollars into these groups to take advantage of America's nonprofit sector and promote Chinese Communist Party propaganda. That much is public. What these groups are fighting to keep hidden is even more concerning," Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., said in a statement. "Either these organizations turn over the documents, or their leaders will answer the Committee's questions under oath." The threatened depositions mark another escalation in a dispute that began with requests for financial records in 2025 and intensified when the committee subpoenaed the three nonprofits in July. The organizations have challenged the investigation, arguing lawmakers are targeting their political views and First Amendment-protected activities. Who could face questioning? The potential deposition targets include eight individuals at The People's Forum, seven at BreakThrough News and six at Tricontinental. Among those named are The People's Forum executive director Manolo De Los Santos, education director Layan Fuleihan and organizing director David Chung; BreakThrough News editor-in-chief Ben Becker, news director Zoe Alexandra and chief correspondent Rania Khalek; and Tricontinental executive director Vijay Prashad and Singham, who is listed as chairman of its international advisory board. The committee has not publicly announced that deposition subpoenas have been issued to any of the individuals. SUBPOENAED PRO-CHINA OUTLET DEFENDS ITSELF ON DEMOCRACY NOW!, WHICH PAID SINGHAM-FOUNDED COMPANY MILLIONS Singham network The panel alleges that Singham channeled money through shell companies and donor-advised funds before it reached the three tax-exempt groups. Such arrangements, the committee said, can allow foreign-linked funding to pass through intermediaries that "by design, obscure the original source of the contribution." Singham is an American-born technology tycoon and longtime Marxist activist who sold his software company, ThoughtWorks, for an estimated $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai. Fox News Digital previously traced at least $278 million from Singham into six core U.S. nonprofits that served as funding hubs within a broader international network of activist groups, media organizations and think tanks promoting socialist, communist and pro-China causes. Of that funding, the investigation found $22.44 million flowed to The People's Forum, $16.76 million to Tricontinental and $1.098 million to BreakThrough BT Media Inc., the parent organization of BreakThrough News. Together, the three received approximately $40.3 million, according to the investigation, which the committee cited in its earlier correspondence. The committee says it is examining whether existing tax laws adequately protect against foreign influence in the nonprofit sector and whether Congress should strengthen those laws. Separately, Singham is under federal grand jury investigation in the Southern District of New York over alleged financial crimes involving his nonprofit funding network, as previously reported by Fox News Digital. The investigation is examining possible wire fraud, bank fraud, money laundering and other financial offenses. No criminal charges against Singham have been announced. WATCH: House subcommittee chair explains Neville Roy Singham's connection to US agitator network BreakThrough News pushes back BreakThrough News condemned the latest demands in an Oct. 9 statement on its website, accusing the committee of targeting its journalists because of their political views. The outlet said it receives no outside editorial direction and that its major donations come from U.S. organizations. During an episode of its BT Live program, hosts Alexandra and Khalek, both named among those facing potential depositions, denounced the committee's demands. "Unless BT gives up its legal rights, including our First Amendment protections, he'll subpoena each of us individually and drag us to Washington for depositions," Alexandra said. Khalek accused lawmakers of targeting journalists personally after the outlet challenged earlier demands. "They will come after us individually if we don't comply with their unconstitutional demands," she said. BreakThrough News also urged supporters to sign a petition opposing the investigation and donate to help cover its legal expenses. Fox News Digital contacted all three organizations and their attorneys for comment on the latest demands but had not received a response as of publication. The investigation has also drawn accusations of McCarthyism from prominent left-wing figures, including Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who called the July subpoenas "the McCarthy trials" and warned, "They will come for you," and CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, who described them as a "terrible attack on independent journalism." ‘MCCARTHY TRIALS’: HASAN PIKER, FAR-LEFT FIGURES ERUPT OVER SUBPOENAS IN $39M SINGHAM PROBE Congressional showdown The committee first sought records from The People's Forum in September 2025 and expanded its investigation to BreakThrough News and Tricontinental in February 2026. After the organizations challenged the requests, lawmakers narrowed their demands in May before issuing subpoenas in July. The committee sought records involving foreign-linked funding, financial arrangements, communications with Singham and other foreign interests, and information about donors and overseas grants. Attorneys for BreakThrough News and The People's Forum formally objected in August, arguing the subpoenas violated First Amendment protections and demanded information beyond the committee's legitimate legislative authority. "A witch-hunt is not a valid legislative purpose," the attorneys wrote in their Aug. 7 responses, comparing the investigation to the House Un-American Activities Committee's investigations of suspected communist influence during the 1940s and 1950s. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The organizations also accused lawmakers of repeatedly changing the stated purpose of the investigation as they challenged earlier requests. Both left open the possibility of responding if the committee narrowed or revised its demands. The committee rejected those arguments, maintaining that its investigation concerns the organizations' finances and structure rather than their political views or journalism.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘Humpty Dumpty’ approach to human rights
articles.summary: The administration insists that policies intended to expand opportunities for historically marginalized groups are themselves discriminatory, a sharp departure from past bipartisan approaches to civil rights.
articles.body:
On Sept. 30, with just hours left to allocate the money in its human rights fund, the State Department directed most of it — more than $175 million — to conservative causes, many of them far removed from the traditional priorities of U.S. foreign policy.

The recipients are not dissidents, journalists or persecuted minorities. Instead, the Trump administration has chosen to support allegedly persecuted whites in South Africa; combat supposed “democratic backsliding” by European allies; and challenge judicial institutions in Brazil accused of censoring conservatives. One program seeks to promote Western “ civilizational values ” by assisting opponents of the European Union’s “supranational and bureaucratic overreach” and restrictions on extremist political speech.

Although the Trump administration has withdrawn the U.S. from major international human rights bodies, treaties and enforcement mechanisms, it continues to employ the language of human rights. Using the approach it has taken to U.S. civil rights law, the administration has turned definitions of victims, discrimination and oppression upside down. And it has largely abandoned the longstanding U.S. commitment to the most fundamental aim of human rights: protecting vulnerable people at home and around the world.

In the process, the administration has greatly undermined America’s moral authority and global stature.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio set the tone when he declared the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor “a platform for left-wing activists to wage vendettas against ‘anti-woke’ leaders” in friendly nations. He established a new Office of Natural Rights to ground U.S. diplomacy in what he called “traditional western conceptions of core freedoms.”

In remarks in Hungary, State Department senior policy adviser Samuel Samson warned that European governments, activist non-profits, and “supranational bodies” were using “technology, courts, and political institutions to restrict patriotic voices, erode national sovereignty, and enforce rigid ideological conformity.” He cited France’s initial refusal to allow Marine Le Pen, head of the far-right National Rally party, to run for president, as well as Germany’s designation of its Alternative für Deutschland party as a “right-wing extremist group.”

Samson neglected to mention that the ban on Le Pen, since lifted, followed her conviction for embezzlement, or that the German intelligence service identified Alternative für Deutschland as extremist because of its hostility toward Germans from Muslim countries.

The newly formed Office of Natural Rights, Samson declared, would reject “novel and ideological ideas” associated with contemporary human rights law and return “to its Western roots.” In practice, this has meant abandoning U.S. leadership of the post-war universalist tradition in favor of right-wing culture-war and white nationalist policies.

Nowhere is this more visible than in the State Department’s revamped annual Country Reports on Human Rights Practices . Instead of focusing on torture, extrajudicial killing and political repression in authoritarian states, the reports now emphasize restrictions against “hate speech” and extremist political parties in democratic countries, including France, Canada and Germany. Attention has been drastically curtailed to violence against women, racial and ethnic violence, gay and transgender rights, government corruption and environmental justice.

Meanwhile, the administration has largely ignored human rights violations by many pro-Trump authoritarian governments. The report on El Salvador , for example, makes the demonstrably false claim that there are “ no credible reports ” there “of significant human rights abuses.”

The connection to the administration’s domestic agenda is clear. U.S. embassies must now treat gender-affirming care, state subsidies for abortion, affirmative action policies and speech-related “official investigations or warnings” as human rights violations. All foreign assistance, including human rights grants, “ must align with State Department policies ” reflecting those views.

At home, the same transformation is underway.

The administration insists that policies intended to expand opportunities for historically marginalized groups are themselves discriminatory, a sharp departure from past bipartisan approaches to civil rights.

The day after returning to office in 2025, President Trump issued an executive order denouncing diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in government, academia and the private sector — not simply as illegal but “dangerous, demeaning, and immoral.” His administration dismantled such federal programs and barred them among federal contractors. He challenged race-conscious policies in higher education and private employment and launched investigations of institutions that continue to pursue diversity initiatives.

After rescinding affirmative-action guidance dating to 1979 that had encouraged employers to improve opportunities for women and minorities, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission invited white men to file workplace discrimination complaints.

In keeping with the administration’s hostility toward “ gender ideology extremism ” and insistence that there are only “ two sexes, male and female ,” the administration has rescinded Title IX guidance protecting transgender students, banned transgender individuals from serving in the military , and insisted that civil rights laws do not cover gender identity .

Every administration pursues its own priorities when addressing human rights abroad and civil rights at home. But despite sometimes sharp differences in approach, Trump’s predecessors largely understood that both bodies of law should serve principally to protect members of historically marginalized groups.

In “Through the Looking Glass,” Humpty Dumpty insisted to Alice that “when I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean — neither more nor less.” The Trump administration seems determined to claim the same prerogative for its mean-spirited and damaging approach to human rights. That said, here’s hoping all the king’s horses and all the king’s men can put human rights together again.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: Trump tries different approach with Russia to bring Americans relief amid ongoing war with Ukraine
articles.summary: Trump's Russian diesel deal faces bipartisan pushback as analysts question whether easing sanctions on Vladimir Putin will lower prices or aid peace.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is easing some of the economic pressure on Russia in hopes of bringing Vladimir Putin closer to a peace deal — a gamble that will test whether economic incentives can move Moscow where years of sanctions have not. The administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel has drawn opposition from Republicans on Capitol Hill and skepticism over whether the move will meaningfully lower prices for Americans. Meanwhile, Russia has offered few public signs of concessions in return. Six Republican senators joined Democrats this week in urging Trump to reverse the decision, while five House Republicans signed a separate bipartisan letter Thursday seeking to revoke the Treasury authorization. The resistance comes as Washington approaches an Oct. 18, 2026, deadline to begin implementing a sweeping new sanctions law Congress overwhelmingly approved to increase economic pressure on Russia. BIPARTISAN SENATORS DEMAND TRUMP SCRAP RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL, CALL IT 'BETRAYAL' OF US ALLIES The administration argues that allowing Russian diesel back onto global markets could help bring down prices for American consumers while demonstrating the economic benefits Russia could gain through improved relations with the United States. Trump has defended the agreement as a way to add supply to a global diesel market strained by high prices, stressing that the Russian fuel does not necessarily need to come state side to benefit American consumers. "That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices," Trump told reporters Tuesday. But energy analysts have questioned whether the volumes involved would meaningfully affect prices. Russia, meanwhile, continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire Sunday. John Hardie, deputy director of the Russia Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, argued the diesel agreement would make more sense as part of a reciprocal deal under which Moscow and Kyiv both stopped attacking energy infrastructure. "The Ukrainians could stomach it if it were part of a mutual energy truce where both Russia and Ukraine don't strike each other's infrastructure," Hardie told Fox News Digital. Instead, Hardie said, Trump pressed Ukraine to halt its refinery strikes without securing the same restraint from Putin. "The better solution is to go back to the Kremlin and try to get that two-way solution," he said. Trump announced the diesel agreement Oct. 9 after a phone call with Putin, saying Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the "American and Global Marketplace," followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons shortly thereafter and eventually another 3 million tons depending on the condition of its refineries. TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET' Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, temporarily authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. The diesel dispute has become part of a broader strain between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, while Zelenskyy has criticized the diesel deal and accused Russia of ignoring Trump's energy ceasefire. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil infrastructure this week after saying Moscow had failed to observe the pause. Russia, meanwhile, has intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy system as winter approaches. A major missile and drone attack Wednesday damaged dozens of energy facilities and left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power, according to Ukrainian officials. The White House says the deal serves two purposes: adding supply to global fuel markets and showing Moscow some of the economic benefits that could come with improved relations. Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the agreement with Ukrainian officials as part of an effort to revive peace negotiations, Reuters reported. One person briefed on the talks said the deal could help "soften" Moscow's position by signaling that Trump remains open to doing business with Russia. But analysts question how much genuinely new diesel Russia can provide. "The amount of diesel Russia can provide would be a drop in the bucket compared to global demand," Masha Kotkin, a fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told S&P Global. "If you are asking about US diesel prices, I don't think it's going to make a difference," she said. Sergey Vakulenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center and former Russian oil executive, similarly cautioned against treating the roughly $7 billion value of the diesel contemplated under the agreement as new revenue for Moscow, noting that Russia was already exporting substantial quantities despite Western sanctions. He estimated the sanctions relief could instead benefit Russian exporters by roughly $30 to $40 per ton through better commercial terms and lower shipping costs — tens of millions of dollars per month, only part of which would reach the Russian state through taxes. At the same time, Ukrainian strikes have sharply constrained Russia's ability to increase supply. Vakulenko said Russian diesel available for export fell from roughly 3 million tons per month in April to about 325,000 tons in September, leaving both Russia's additional financial benefit and the deal's potential impact on global prices more limited than the headline figures suggest. Hardie said signs of division between Washington and Kyiv could encourage Putin to increase military pressure rather than compromise. "That message of irresolution and of division between Washington and Kyiv only encourages Putin to intensify military pressure, kind of seeing that opportunity," Hardie said. He said the administration had previously presented sanctions relief and renewed economic ties as benefits Russia could unlock through a negotiated settlement. Offering some of those benefits beforehand, he warned, could undermine that incentive. "It'll lead Putin to kind of digging his heels in on maximalist demands," Hardie said. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law Sept. 18, giving the administration new authorities to target Russian officials, financial institutions and entities helping sustain the war. Vice President Vance claimed Saturday that in “some ways” the United States has “decisively won” its war against Iran .

“I would say in some ways, we have won decisively, but they’re — the Iranians, the enemy gets a vote here, and they have responded in certain ways. And so, to step back a little bit, why did the president of the United States do this?” Vance told CBS News’s Tony Dokoupil in a town hall.

“The president of the United States did this because he believes it is very important, and I think he’s right, I think most people here would agree, even if they don’t agree with all the particulars of the policy, to say Iran, the largest state sponsor of terrorism in the world, cannot have a nuclear weapon,” the vice president added.

Vance’s comments come only a few weeks out from the midterms, in which he and his party are facing rough political territory with issues including the unpopular war in Iran. The conflict has driven up energy prices as the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed amid the fighting

The war in Iran is set to reach the eight-month mark in a little under two weeks.

According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of gas on Sunday morning was about $4.30, up from about $3.04 last year at the same time.

President Trump’s approval rating has also sagged amid the war in Iran, with his rating sitting at 39.8 percent on Sunday morning, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, and his disapproval rating sitting at 58.7 percent.

articles.title: U.S. taking Putin’s side would be a ‘historic mistake,’ says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill. “We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.” Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month, the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas. The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar. At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.” The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across four and a half years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each offering public criticisms of the other. Asked about Trump’s remark this week that the Ukrainian leader was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump. “Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.” Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said that his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.” Announcing the deal week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs. But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine. “I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said. Of the prospect of the U.S. more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.” Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.” “He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said. In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions. “He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices. Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford said that Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.” The war has seen little recent movement on the frontline, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender. Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes. Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said. He cited some progress after a multiday interruption to U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.” “We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.” European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks. While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said that Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service. Asked if he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said that he didn’t know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
