articles.title: Poll: Americans are anxious, pessimistic and deeply unhappy with Trump ahead of the midterms
articles.summary: Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.”
articles.body: Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey. Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. For the first time in Trump’s second term, the poll has found the “right track” sinking into the 20s. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions. Trump’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. In another warning sign, the poll found a majority (51%) of respondents “strongly disapprove” of his performance, a second-term high. Trump’s approval rating is slightly better among registered voters, 39%-61%. Registered voters said they prefer Democrats over Republicans to control Congress by a 55%-45% spread, another sign that the GOP’s House and Senate majorities are in danger in the Nov. 3 election. Yet despite the sinking ratings for the party in power, Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably, while 57% hold an unfavorable view. The survey found that 37% have a favorable opinion of the Republican Party, while 63% view it unfavorably. The president’s approval rating is 76% with Republican adults. That represents a drop from his previous numbers among members of his own party, fueled by a decline among Republicans who consider themselves more a supporter of the party than a supporter of the MAGA movement. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating sits at 21% with independents. Among men under 30 — a group Trump won by 1 point in 2024 exit polling — his approval rating sits at 28%. And among Latinos, who also shifted toward Trump in 2024, his approval rating is 31%. The poll highlights the tricky balancing act facing Republican candidates in competitive states and districts as they simultaneously try to energize GOP voters who continue to support Trump without alienating Americans who disapprove of the administration. Among adults, 58% said Trump’s policies are hurting the country, while 28% said they are helping the country. Another 14% said they aren’t making a difference. When broken down by issues, Trump’s approval rating is 27% on handling the cost of living, 29% on handling the war with Iran and 33% on his handling of AI. On his best issue, border security and immigration, 43% of adults approve. Economic concerns are at the center of the sour national mood, with the economy once again topping the list of most important issues at 31%. While 18% of Americans said their financial situation is better off today than a year ago, 38% said it’s about the same and 44% said it’s worse now. The results provided detail on how rising inflation, which last month rose to 3.7% year over year, has weighed on Americans’ daily lives. Gas prices were described as a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem by 67% of respondents. Majorities said economic conditions have caused them to change what groceries they buy to live within their means, and to cut back on spending to afford necessities. Pluralities also said they’ve cut back on electricity use, changed or canceled travel plans or delayed a major purchase as a result, according to the poll. Trump has sought to appeal to voters by promising $5,000 payments if Republicans win the 2026 midterms. But the new poll showed that most U.S. adults aren’t buying it: Just 14% said they “definitely” or “probably” expect to receive such a check if the GOP keeps control of Congress, while 71% think they “definitely” or “probably” won’t. Self-identified Republicans are among those who don’t appear to buy the president’s pledge, with 47% saying they don’t expect to receive the $5,000 payment Trump promised, while 28% do. Corruption also registered as a major concern, with Americans harboring skepticism about both parties. More than half (52%) of U.S. adults said in the poll that they find his administration “more corrupt” than previous administrations, while about 1 in 4 said it’s less corrupt and another 1 in 4 said the current administration is about as corrupt as predecessors. A 56% majority also said corruption is equally bad in both parties, while another 25% said it’s a bigger problem inside the GOP and 17% said it’s worse among Democrats. The dissatisfaction may be reshaping what Americans want in a politician. In another edition of this poll one year ago, Americans said by a 16-point margin they prefer an insider with the experience to get things done over an outsider who shakes up the system. That margin narrowed to 4 points in the new poll. Among Democrats, the survey also found indicators of diminishing trust in the party’s establishment and an openness to different kinds of candidates. When asked to pick one or the other, 52% of self-identified Democrats said they’re more of a supporter of progressive causes and the progressive movement, while 48% said they’re more of a supporter of the Democratic Party. Among Democratic-aligned adults, 42% said they consider themselves to be democratic socialists, while 58% said they do not. And despite Trump’s unpopularity, the country was split almost evenly on whether a potential Democratic-led House should begin impeachment proceedings: 52% said it should, while 48% said it should not go down that path. The NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey surveyed 19,135 adults online from Sept. 28 to Oct. 12 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points.

articles.title: The nine key races that will decide who controls the Senate, and where they stand
articles.summary: Democrats eye multiple paths to flip the Senate majority as six toss-up races across Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas shape Election Day.
articles.body: Democrats have expanded their once-narrow path to reclaiming the Senate majority with just over two weeks until Election Day, but they'll need to win several competitive races to take control of the chamber. If Democrats ride a massive blue wave in the midterm elections, they could end up with 52 or even 53 seats in the next Senate. But if Republicans out-perform the polls, they could hold their majority, which currently stands at 53-47. Here's a look at the current battlefield and both parties' routes to securing a Senate majority in the midterms. The latest Power Rankings point to Democrats and Republicans each taking 47 seats in the midterms, leaving six races rated as true toss-ups. Additionally, three races are rated as leaners — one step shy of a toss-up. These nine showdowns will likely determine whether the Democrats make a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate or if the GOP holds the majority. DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE "Nine races will determine control of the Senate, and on the polling alone, you could call any of them toss-ups," said Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings. The GOP is fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. Republicans also face a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. With Republicans controlling the seats in six of the nine competitive races in the Power Rankings, the GOP is playing more defense than the Democrats. The six toss-up states are Alaska, where Sen. Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Democratic challenger and former Rep. Mary Peltola; Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson is trying to keep retiring Sen. Joni Ernst's seat in GOP hands against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek; and Maine, where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is running for re-election against former state Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT Also on the list is Ohio, where appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted is running to serve the final two years of the term won in 2022 by now-Vice President JD Vance. He's facing former longtime Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton is battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in the race to succeed longtime GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who was ousted by Paxton in a bitter Republican primary. Democrats are playing defense in Michigan, the sixth toss-up, where nominee Abdul El-Sayed is trying to keep party control of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters' seat, as he faces former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Democrats are also on defense in New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is aiming to keep retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat blue against former GOP Sen. John E. Sununu. The Power Rankings rate the race "Lean Democrat." It's a similar story in Minnesota, where Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is trying to keep retiring Sen. Tina Smith's seat in party hands. But the Power Rankings this past week shifted the race in the blue-leaning state toward the GOP, from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat, as Republican nominee Michele Tafoya appears to gain traction. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Meanwhile, the GOP is on defense in red-leaning Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a difficult re-election fight against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, a pastor. The Power Rankings rate the race Lean Republican. Numa, pointing to Kansas, Minnesota and New Hampshire, said that "the voter profiles and histories of those states are keeping them at 'Lean D' and 'Lean R' on the forecast, but this map has expanded, and with the exception of the North Star State, mostly into red territory." Meanwhile, two states are now pretty much off the table for the GOP. Georgia was a top Republican target when the 2026 cycle began, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff holds a solid lead over GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins in the southeastern battleground. Republican outside groups have cut their spending significantly in Georgia, and the Fox News Power Rankings rate the race as Likely Democrat. In neighboring North Carolina, Republicans appear to have conceded the seat held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Republican groups have pulled the plug on spending on behalf of GOP nominee Mike Whatley, who trails former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, in polling. The Fox News Power Rankings also rate this race as Likely Democrat. The Democrats win the majority if they run the table by holding Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, and flip North Carolina as well as at least three of the five GOP-controlled toss-up states. "Senate Democrats are in the strongest position yet to win the majority – with multiple paths to flip GOP-held seats and growing momentum across the map," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, touted in a recent statement. Conversely, Republicans would keep control of the chamber by holding at least three of the toss-ups where they're playing defense. A 50-50 Senate would remain in GOP hands, thanks to the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance. Gillibrand's counterpart, National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, remains optimistic. "I think it's going very well for us," Scott said Thursday in an interview on Fox News "America Reports." "The momentum, frankly, is with us, not against us." The GOP majority could be bolstered if the party goes on offense. While chances of Sununu flipping New Hampshire appear to be receding, Republicans are optimistic Rogers can top El-Sayed in Michigan. Trump is expected to hold a rally with Rogers in the Great Lakes battleground later this month. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meanwhile, Scott has his eyes on a flip in Minnesota. "Michele Tafoya is running a very independent campaign, lots of traction," he told Fox News. "I think we close that gap. And if there's an October surprise, Minnesota goes Republican."

articles.title: Homan says investigators have a ‘strong case’ against Omar
articles.summary: White House border czar Tom Homan said federal investigators have a “strong case” in the ongoing criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) for possible immigration fraud after federal agents raided her home last week. In an interview with Fox News on Saturday, Homan said he was informed by investigators that they have been following…
articles.body:
White House border czar Tom Homan said federal investigators have a “strong case” in the ongoing criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) for possible immigration fraud after federal agents raided her home last week.

In an interview with Fox News on Saturday, Homan said he was informed by investigators that they have been following strong pieces of evidence in the wake of the multiple court authorized search warrants on Omar’s Washington, D.C. home.

“If she violated law then she’d be held accountable,” Homan said, adding that she will not be receiving any special treatment throughout the investigation.

Omar has not been charged with a crime and has denied the allegations, calling the investigation politically motivated.

In a separate interview on Thursday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin denied claims that the investigation was politically motivated.

“We wouldn’t move forward, and President Trump didn’t want to move forward either, unless we knew that it couldn’t be politically driven,” Mullin said in an interview with “The Charlie Kirk Show” host Andrew Kolvet. “This individual wants to try making it about themselves. This was about enforcing once again our nation’s laws, and it’s a strong case.”

The probe stems from numerous allegations levied by President Trump and other GOP figures that allege Omar’s immigration documents submitted by her family decades ago may be fraudulent.

Multiple members of Omar’s family, including her brother and her sister, were subpoenaed as part of the investigation, and her cell phone was reportedly confiscated.

Mullin also described the ongoing investigation as a “strong case,” suggesting Omar could also be prosecuted for possible coordinated immigration fraud under federal racketeering laws.

In the Thursday interview, he presented a hypothetical scenario in which a person filled out their paperwork unlawfully and allowed others to enter the country under them.

“Then that can be considered a RICO case, right?” he said. “Because there was conspiracy to deceive the American government, and therefore everything else that came in with it could then be looked at [part of] the same case.”

articles.title: Obama backs Ilhan Omar amid probe, accuses Trump admin of 'appalling' targeting in lengthy statement
articles.summary: Barack Obama accused the Trump administration of politically targeting Rep. Ilhan Omar, alleging efforts to strip her citizenship and deport her.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama accused the Trump administration of weaponizing the federal government against its political enemies in a social media post defending Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., amid an investigation into the progressive lawmaker's citizenship. Obama claimed the administration is attempting to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and deport her over her criticism of President Donald Trump, warning that the effort could set a dangerous precedent. "It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say," Obama wrote Sunday on X. "But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota." ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS Obama's remarks come after federal agents searched Omar's Washington, D.C., home as part of a criminal investigation into her immigration status. Sources previously told Fox News Digital that investigators are examining whether Omar or her father committed fraud on immigration paperwork when she became a U.S. citizen decades ago. Obama defended the circumstances under which Omar became a U.S. citizen, saying, "To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts." Obama then said Omar arrived in the United States with her father at age 12 and automatically became a citizen at 17 when her father was naturalized. The former president accused investigators of pursuing an "unsubstantiated theory" that Omar was actually 18 at the time, which he said would have required her to apply for citizenship separately. "The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," Obama wrote. Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House and Department of Homeland Security for comment on the former president's allegations. Trump has denied involvement in the investigation, previously telling reporters that the matter was up to the Justice Department. "I've always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said. Obama also accused the administration of repeatedly targeting perceived political opponents, pointing to federal actions involving New York's attorney general, a former FBI director and members of the Federal Reserve. "The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views," Obama wrote. articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers (R) on Sunday said he’s worried about the “optics” of the U.S.’s deal with Russia to export diesel and added that the U.S. cannot give Russian President Vladimir Putin “an inch.”

Rogers told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union” that President Trump is “trying to do something to bring down diesel prices” by striking a deal with Russia.

“I do worry about the optics of it, but I understand what his motives are and his motives are, ‘Try to get prices back down on diesel, diesel’s hurting us,'” Rogers said.

The former lawmaker later said he would have voted for the sanctions package signed into law last month, posthumously dedicated to the late Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-S.C.). The law’s intent is to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its years-long military operations against Ukraine by imposing tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and those who help the country evade sanctions.

“I don’t think we can give Putin an inch, and we’ll see –– if the strategy works, hey, good on them, because that means we’re going to pay less for diesel in the United States,” Rogers said.

The Michigan Republican said if Trump has a “better idea” to lower diesel prices, “I’d be for it.”

“I’m just a little skeptical that this will work the way that the administration wants it to work,” he said. “And we’re paying a pretty heavy price here in Michigan. We’ve got to get these prices down, which is why I call to –– hey, it’s time to wrap up the Iran conflict. We’ve got to get this thing settled.”

“Our initial objectives have been met,” Rogers added. “Let’s wrap it up. Let’s get these prices back down. Let’s get people putting a little more money in their wallets.”

Rogers has been among the GOP candidates running in the midterm elections to call for the conflict to end to lower gas prices. He said in a campaign ad last month that Michigan families cannot “afford to wait” for the war to end for prices to go down.

On Friday, Trump issued an executive order waiving sanctions against Russia set to take effect soon as part of the sanctions package. Trump said he “submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”

The diesel deal would have Russia, according to Trump, “immediately” begin supplying 300,000 tons of diesel, an additional 500,000 tons in November and then one million tons “immediately thereafter.” The deal elicited bipartisan backlash on Capitol Hill, with five Republican lawmakers joining their Democratic colleagues to denounce the relief.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a “birthday gift” to Putin and said Wednesday that he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decision. He said Saturday that Ukraine is open to negotiating for an end to the conflict and urged the U.S. to pressure Russia, not his country.

“Otherwise, it’s simply unfair,” he said on the social platform X.

articles.title: Treasury secretary refuses to say if the U.S. sees Ukraine as an ally
articles.summary: Amid escalating tensions between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday dodged three times when asked whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States.
articles.body: Amid escalating tensions between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday dodged three times when asked whether Ukraine is an ally of the United States. “We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” Bessent told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” the second time he was asked whether the U.S. considers Ukraine an ally. Asked for a third time, the treasury secretary simply said, “I’m not the secretary of state. I’m not the president.” Earlier, Bessent said the U.S. supports Ukraine in three keys ways, including providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing NATO to purchases U.S. weapons to resell to Ukraine. He then accused Europe of falling short in its support for Ukraine, saying: “When President Zelenskyy asked for Patriots [missile systems], NATO — the European members of NATO — they have plenty of Patriots. Why aren’t they forthcoming with the Patriots?” Bessent’s comments came shortly after Zelenskyy appeared on the program and told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker that it would be a “historic mistake” for the U.S. to side with Russia in the ongoing war. The Ukrainian president, who has had a sometimes tense and sometimes friendly relationship with the U.S. president, said of Trump that “we want to trust him” and “I hope that he will change his decisions.” The current tension between the U.S. and Ukrainian leaders comes after Trump last weekend said that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” a move that caught some European allies by surprise. For days, Zelenskyy halted Ukraine’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure but insisted that Russia was not abiding by the same agreement. Days ago, Ukraine’s military resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries and accused the U.S. of withholding intelligence about incoming Russian strikes that the U.S. normally shares with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also accused tech mogul and Trump ally Elon Musk of limiting the country’s access to Starlink, which Ukraine uses to track drones and defend itself. In his “Meet the Press,” interview, Zelenskyy said Starlink speed limitations are interfering with Ukrainian forces’ ability to block drones and that he believes the decision to limit the speed was a “message from American government.” The Ukrainian president also told “Meet the Press” that intelligence-sharing from the U.S. was blocked for a period of time. Trump denied that the U.S. had stopped sharing certain intelligence, and Starlink services later resumed at normal speed. On Sunday, Bessent criticized Zelenskyy for publicly accusing the U.S. and Musk of limiting his resources in the war, saying: “President Trump and Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.” On Friday, the U.S. president also announced he would waive certain sanctions on Russia that were recently approved by Congress in a bipartisan vote. Earlier in the month, Trump said he would allow Russia “immediately” to begin selling hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel on the global market. On Sunday, Bessent denied that Trump lifted any sanctions, instead telling “Meet the Press” that the president wanted a 60-day pause “so we can examine what’s going on.” “The only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo,” he added. The treasury secretary also accused Zelenskyy of presenting a “false binary” about the war in his earlier interview. “President Trump has made it clear that he wants to end this war; that it must stop. And President Zelenskyy presented a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent said. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement. And President Trump is working on that every day.”

articles.title: MAP: Did your state try to stop changing the clocks this year?
articles.summary: Lawmakers across the U.S. tried to keep their clocks from changing this year.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – We’re just weeks away from changing our clocks as daylight saving time comes to an end. If lawmakers in several states had their way this year, their clocks may not be changing.

Daylight saving time ends as early as possible this year , with clocks “falling back” an hour in the early morning hours of Nov. 1.

The House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent, but it has stalled out in the Senate . The chamber is adjourned until mid-November, and there are doubts that the legislation has the support needed to pass .

The legislation, known as the Sunshine Protection Act, is the critical piece of legislation for the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time within their jurisdiction. States can opt for permanent standard time, as two already have , but year-round daylight saving time requires Congressional action.

Several states tried to make standard time their year-round time this year, but efforts mostly failed, fizzled or were flattened by the end of the legislative session.

In Virginia, the state Senate passed a bill that would make standard time permanent, so long as the District of Columbia and Maryland do the same. While neither has taken action on that, Virginia’s bill will carry over to its 2027 legislative session.

Standard time-related legislation in Pennsylvania , New Jersey and Michigan is still active, as their lawmakers are still in session.

Meanwhile, tracking by Nexstar shows more than 100 pieces of state legislation were introduced during this year’s legislative session.

The interactive map shows where that legislation was introduced.

Only a few remain active, including legislation in New Jersey and Pennsylvania . Separate bills in Pennsylvania and Ohio would urge Congress to make daylight saving time permanent in the U.S.

Health experts generally agree that we should lock our clocks on permanent standard time , despite federal efforts largely focusing on making daylight saving time permanent .

Not everyone supports the shift to permanent daylight saving time, either. It could impact how thousands practice their religion . It could have “considerable implications” on your future flights , at least temporarily.

It’s difficult to say when, if ever, the Senate will pick up the Sunshine Protection Act. Efforts by the Senate to fast-track its version were thwarted .

Congress is also considering two bills in the House that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, a bill to make half-daylight saving time permanent , and a newly introduced bill to make standard time permanent , with exceptions.

articles.title: The public execution is off, but it never should have gotten this far
articles.summary: They didn’t change their minds; they lost the argument.
articles.body:
The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman.

According to a recent NPR report , “Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers built gallows near the riverfront.” The night before, in what “historians describe as a festive atmosphere,” attendees “celebrated with ‘ necktie ’ parties” and “sipped soft drinks.”

“They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Cola, and you’d have thought it was a big picnic or something,” said an attendee during a 2013 oral history interview with the county library.

Despite the celebratory mood in Owensboro, the national outrage was clear. There have been no public executions in the U.S. since 1938. Eighty-eight years later, this administration came within weeks of ending that streak.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan on Dec. 3 would be livestreamed for the public, and President Trump said he “ absolutely ” approved. Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, murdered 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

On Thursday, after bipartisan backlash, Trump reversed course . The execution will not be streamed, and I’m glad. But we should be honest about what happened: They didn’t change their minds; they just lost the argument.

Even in retreat, Trump insisted that broadcasting a man’s death “might have been a strong deterrent.” It is worth remembering that this was the plan.

I served as a South Carolina prosecutor for more than a decade. Bound by my oath to uphold the laws of this state, I persuaded a jury to sentence a man to die in the electric chair. In another case, I stood before the U.S. Supreme Court on behalf of the state of South Carolina and argued for the execution of another convicted man. Years later, as a state senator, I introduced and helped pass a law authorizing the firing squad as a means of imposing the death penalty in South Carolina. I did it because I believed it was more humane than electrocution.

I told the story of the Donald “Pee Wee” Gaskins case in my book, “Dig Me a Grave.” Writing it forced me to confront what it means for the state to take a life, and what that responsibility demands of the people who carry it out. And although I support the death penalty, I support it only in the narrowest of circumstances.

I have spent my career on both sides of the courtroom, as a prosecutor and as a defense attorney. Execution by any method is not and never has been an effective deterrent to crime. Putting it on a screen will not change that.

Execution is a deterrent to the condemned person’s further criminal conduct. Gaskins, the man I sent to the electric chair, had been convicted of 13 prior murders and then assassinated a man on death row just because he could. It was time for him to go; time to end his propensity for murder.

And don’t get me wrong: It is also Hasan’s time to go. But a public display of his death wouldn’t have punished him as much as it would have punished us. While invited, I did not attend the execution of the man I convicted. Had I attended, I believe that I would have fallen to his level.

I understand victims who attend executions. They believe it will give them closure, although I have never personally witnessed that effect. There is no joy or sense of accomplishment in the taking of a human life. Those who wanted to make a spectacle of it are — and I say this seriously — more like the condemned than the victim. There might have been parties and gatherings to watch a man in a wheelchair get shot to death. How would we have explained to them why we chose to make death a form of public entertainment?

It’s clear that Trump and Hegseth revel in releasing footage of hellfire raining down on anonymous people they have summarily declared the enemy. But those videos are too clinical and too antiseptic, and the ratings aren’t good enough. So, the former reality show host wanted his own “Hunger Games,” where the country could watch death unfold in real time.

Viewers could have replayed it in slow motion and watched the blood erupt as the bullets hit. The more gruesome the footage, the higher the ratings.

That is the lesson this White House was prepared to teach America: A life is worth nothing, and character doesn’t matter. That they were stopped this time doesn’t mean they’ve learned anything.

Dick Harpootlian, former chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party , is a defense attorney and founder of Harpootlian Attorneys At Law. He is a former South Carolina state senator and a former prosecutor who led the case against serial killer Donald “Pee Wee” Gaskins. He is the author of “ Dig Me a Grave .”

articles.title: Pence calls on Trump to restore sanctions, scrap Russia diesel deal
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence on Sunday called for President Trump to restore sanctions on Russia and condemned his recent diesel agreement with President Vladimir Putin. “President Trump’s decision to waive sanctions against Russia as Putin continues his brutal war of aggression against Ukraine dishonors the legacy of the late Senator Lindsey Graham and is…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence on Sunday called for President Trump to restore sanctions on Russia and condemned his recent diesel agreement with President Vladimir Putin.

“President Trump’s decision to waive sanctions against Russia as Putin continues his brutal war of aggression against Ukraine dishonors the legacy of the late Senator Lindsey Graham and is decidedly not in the national interests of the United States and should be reversed,” the former vice president wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“Putin is a war criminal and only understands strength. Waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia signals weakness at a moment that demands American strength. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression, just as we did during the years of the first Trump Administration,” he added.

On Friday, Trump signed an executive order waiving specific sanctions within the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a legislation package designed to pressure Russia into ending its years-long war against Ukraine.

The president announced earlier this month his intention to lift sanctions on Russia following a conversation with Putin, allowing 300,000 tons of Russian oil to supply the U.S. and global economies.

The decision — which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called “ gifts to Putin ” — has been met with intense backlash.

“This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote on X in response to the announcement .

Republicans have also criticized it. On Thursday, five House GOP lawmakers joined Democratic colleagues in calling for Trump to cancel the deal.

But the president and other Trump administration officials have not yet yielded to critical members of their party.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday defended the president’s decision .

“This is a carrot to try to end a war,” Wright said in an interview on ABC News’s “This Week.” “It’s not an economic lifeline for Russia.”

articles.title: Obama: Omar investigation should ‘outrage all Americans’
articles.summary: Former President Obama has weighed in on the federal government’s criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) over accusations of immigration fraud, accusing the Trump administration of targeting its political opponents. In a lengthy post on the social platform X, Obama claimed the probe was an attempt to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and…
articles.body:
Former President Obama has weighed in on the federal government’s criminal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) over accusations of immigration fraud, accusing the Trump administration of targeting its political opponents.

In a lengthy post on the social platform X , Obama claimed the probe was an attempt to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and possibly deport her over her public criticisms of President Trump.

“It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say,” Obama said. “But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.”

Obama’s remarks come nearly a week after federal agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home and seized her phone as part of a criminal investigation into her immigration paperwork.

Following accusations from Trump and other GOP figures of immigration fraud, investigators are examining whether Omar or her father provided false information during their naturalization process when she was a child.

No charges have been filed against the Minnesota Democrat, and she has denied all allegations, claiming she is being politically targeted.

Obama also refuted the allegations, saying Omar, who was born in Somalia, arrived in the U.S. with her father when she was 12 and automatically became a citizen when she was 17 after her father was naturalized.

He accused the administration of pursuing an “unsubstantiated theory” that Omar was actually 18 at the time, which would have required her to apply for citizenship separately.

“The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president,” Obama said.

Trump has denied involvement in the investigation, previously telling reporters that the matter was up to the Justice Department.

“I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said.

Obama also cited federal investigations involving New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and former FBI director James Comey as examples of what he described as the administration’s pattern of targeting perceived political enemies.

He said those cases had either stalled or been dismissed and predicted that the investigation into Omar would face a similar outcome.

“But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota,” he said.

“If this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.”

NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE "If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump wrote. articles.title: We must fix our broken prison system
articles.summary: The article highlights the critical need for enhanced rehabilitation and educational programs within the prison system to combat high recidivism rates, building upon the foundation of the First Step Act.
articles.body:
Recidivism rates in this country are a sign of the abject failure of our justice and prison system.

The U.S. has close to 4.2 percent of the world’s population but almost 20 percent of the world’s prisoners. And almost 70 percent of U.S. prisoners are rearrested within three years after they are released. Prison is meant to be a punishment. It is meant to get dangerous criminals off the streets. And the threat of prison can be a deterrent to committing crimes.

But the prison system should also try to rehabilitate the mostly young and minority men who commit stupid and dangerous crimes when they reach their teen years. Lock up a 19-year-old male for crimes and he is likely to come out of prison in a few years unskilled, unhirable, addicted to drugs, and with few skills learned in prison except how to be a career criminal.

Some veer away from crime, but most turn back to it for a lack of many viable alternatives.

President Trump has already taken some heroic steps to reverse these terribly depressing trends with his First Step program to lead prisoners away from crime.

There are also many private efforts to train and educate prison inmates to achieve that goal — but they are underutilized.

There have been commendable efforts from the likes of Tony Lowden on the left, a lifetime confidant of President Jimmy Carter and champion of prison reform. Over on the right, a senior official in the Department of Education, David Barker, Ph.D., is also working inside the Trump administration to train the incarcerated so that they come out of prison with useful skills.

There is a small percentage of violent people behind bars who need to be kept off the streets for the safety of citizens. But what do we do about the thousands of inmates rotting in prison who do not fit into this category?

They sleep, watch television and often join gangs that provide them with drugs as the only escape from an awful existence. They should be learning employable skills — carpentry, welding, construction, auto repair, etc. — that help make them employable when they are done serving their time.

Instead, we have created a “Prison Industrial Complex” where corruption is rampant and inmates are treated like cattle.

Maybe we should be providing prison officials hefty raises and bonuses based on their track record of holding down recidivism rates. In other words, they should be paid for their performance in ensuring that the correctional institutions they run truly correct these prisoners’ ways.

Education, training, healthcare and restoration are ignored for the majority of prisoners. Retention rates soar for inmates learning in prison classrooms by orders of magnitude when content is viewed on a virtual reality headset. Distractions vanish. Brain synapses are both relaxed and catalyzed to intake instruction. Shame, probably the greatest impediment in adults’ vocational education programs, is minimized. Technology now exists for prisoners to earn a high school diploma, college degree, or certifications in electrical, plumbing and HVAC.

Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) and Amy Frizzell, director of Programs and Re-Entry of the Florida Department of Corrections, are shining examples of leaders tackling recidivism. Down in the U.S. Virgin Islands, the recidivism rate is only 11 percent thanks to the leadership of Bureau of Corrections Director Wynnie Testamark.

In the 19th century, Frederick Douglass advanced the idea that education is the key to the pursuit of human thriving. He would be both aghast at present recidivism rates, and encouraged by the multitude of organizations taking shape to radically reduce those rates.

In 2018, Trump signed the bipartisan First Step Act , a monumental criminal justice reform bill written to promote rehabilitation, lower recidivism, and shorten lengthy sentences in federal prisons. A vast coalition of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle and advocacy groups championed the bill as a major step in fixing excessive sentences handed out in the 1980s and 1990s.

The First Step Act created more opportunities for federal prisoners to attend rehabilitative programs to help them after they get released. This included new education programs.

The Trump administration has a golden opportunity to add to the great strides they made last term with the First Step Act by supporting modern technology to help equip prisoners so they can lead productive, and happy lives. Think about how much money will be saved by transforming them into employed taxpayers.

Stephen Moore is a former senior economic advisor to President Trump and now serves as CEO of Unleash Prosperity. He is an Advisory Board member of Promising People . John L. Evans Jr., Ed.D., is co-founder of Promising People.

articles.title: Slotkin wants GOP prosecutions to deter young people from Trump administration jobs
articles.summary: Elissa Slotkin said she wants young people to fear legal problems before joining the Trump administration, sparking fierce online backlash..
articles.body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is facing online backlash after saying she wants the threat of prosecution to make young people think twice before taking jobs in the Trump administration. During an Oct. 13 University of Chicago event focused on her political path and the future of the Democratic Party, Slotkin said she wants to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" President Donald Trump. "I want to look at these signature cases and not just focus on the president, but on the people who enabled him," the Michigan Democrat said. Slotkin went on to describe how she wants prospective administration employees to weigh the risks. "I want young people coming out of school to say, should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity. I want them to be like, Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that," she said. "I want that deterrence message." MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD Law professor Jonathan Turley criticized the remarks on X, writing that Slotkin had "said the quiet part out loud." He argued that she wants to deter young people from supporting the administration. The remarks were made during a University of Chicago event focused on Slotkin’s political path and the future of the Democratic Party. A clip of the exchange circulated online, prompting critics to accuse her of trying to scare potential administration employees away from public service. Scott Kupor, director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, which manages the federal government’s civilian workforce, called Slotkin’s comments "disappointing and unprofessional." "This is incredibly disappointing and unprofessional coming from a U.S. senator — endorsing political prosecutions to dissuade patriotic Americans from serving their country," Kupor wrote on X. "In contrast, we at OPM believe in recruiting the best and brightest early-career prospects." Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student, said Slotkin’s remarks made him and other conservative students feel they could face political persecution for serving in the Trump administration. REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE "Sen. Slotkin, a self-avowed "defender of democracy," told me and other conservative students that we should live in fear of political persecution if we dare serve our country in the Trump administration. Sadly for her, we will never be intimidated by her Bolshevik-style tactics," he wrote on X. The debate over Slotkin’s remarks unfolded as former President Barack Obama criticized the Trump administration’s scrutiny of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., arguing she was being targeted for her political views. "The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views," Obama wrote on X. One commenter accused Obama of overlooking what they saw as a parallel: Slotkin’s call for investigations of Trump administration officials. Omar is facing two separate federal inquiries: federal agents searched her Washington home as part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork, while D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office was examining Omar’s financial disclosures after businesses tied to her husband reported a sharp increase in value. It remains unclear whether the probes are connected. articles.title: Pro-Israel leader warns Democrats failing to condemn ‘vicious Jew haters’ in Congress
articles.summary: Democratic Sen.-nominee Abdul El-Sayed's refusal to call Iran a bigger threat than Israel at a Michigan Senate debate alarmed ZOA's Morton Klein.
articles.body: When Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed could not say Iran is a bigger threat to the U.S. than Israel, it was a warning of elections in a post-Oct. 7 world, Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) president Morton Klein says. American and even Israeli leaders are failing to show strength against hate as anti-Zionist voices gain power, Klein told Fox News Digital in a Monday interview. "Ilhan Omar is one of the most vicious Jew haters in America," Klein said, speaking on behalf of himself and not as the leader of the ZOA. "And it is very painful to me that the leaders of the Democratic Party have not continuously and vigorously condemned her" and other antisemitic political leaders, including Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. They are not merely "pro-Palestinian" voices, Klein says: "They're anti-Israel voices. They don't really give a damn about the Palestinians either. They just hate Jews in the Jewish state. That's my opinion." RESCUE EXPERT WARNS FLYDUBAI HIJACKING ATTEMPT SHOWS US, ALLIES ARE ‘PLAYING CHECKERS’ AGAINST TERROR THREAT The ZOA is a 501(c)(3) that is unpermitted by law to talk candidacies as opposed to their positions, Klein stressed, before unloading on the voices that take aim at Israel and ostensibly handing political power to the antisemites and terrorists – which even includes Israeli elections just two weeks from now. "Viciously antisemitic members of Congress have not been condemned in any significant way by the Democratic Party," he continued. "So it's disappointing to me as an American that we don't condemn people who are filled with hate and not filled with what's best for America." Anti-Israel rhetoric has moved from the political fringe into elected office, he said, warning that Democrats have not forcefully condemned members of their own party who he says traffic in antisemitism. TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS It has even forced Israeli leaders to move toward a dangerous level of "appeasement," according to Klein. "I blame the Jewish leaders and the Israeli leaders themselves: You might find that surprising," he said. "The Israeli government over the years has not made it clear that the Hamas Charter has two clauses that say, murder every Jew on earth, destroy Israel. And, most recently, El-Sayed not only refused to clearly name Iran, the world's leading state sponsor of terror, as a greater threat than Israel during a Michigan Senate debate, "he said worse," Klein lamented. articles.title: Photos show aftermath of riots as masked groups clash with police across France
articles.summary: Paris streets littered with burned cars and shattered storefronts as police report 1,800 arrests nationwide following violent clashes over living costs.
articles.body: Paris woke Sunday to shattered storefronts, burned cars and a heavy police presence after unrest swept through the city and other parts of France. Violent clashes broke out Saturday during nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and poor school conditions. Hundreds of thousands marched across the country, while masked groups fought with police, looted businesses and set fires in several cities. Police reported 1,800 arrests nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED The destruction was not limited to Paris. In Limoges, about three hours south of the capital, fire tore through the city’s historic town hall, built in 1883 and designated a historic landmark in 1975. The local prefect, Maurice Barate, told AFP that the roof had collapsed onto the lower floors and about two-thirds of the building’s exterior had disappeared. He called it "a catastrophe for heritage." LIMOGES TOWN HALL ‘LARGELY LOST’ AFTER FAR-LEFT RIOTERS SET HISTORIC BUILDING ON FIRE French President Emmanuel Macron had called for "calm and respect" ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the right to protest must be exercised with respect for people and property. But as violence escalated, the French president and his wife, Brigitte, were spotted at a Celine Dion concert in Nanterre, west of Paris, according to French media reports. The couple reportedly arrived and left discreetly and joined roughly 35,000 spectators at the Plenitude Arena. Macron had spent Thursday and Friday in Brussels for a European Council meeting. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED President Donald Trump weighed in Sunday, blaming immigration for the unrest in a Truth Social post and urging France to close its borders. articles.title: I worked for 3 White House press secretaries — here’s some advice for the next one
articles.summary: Former Reagan White House staffer Mark Weinberg offers advice to the incoming U.S. press secretary by reflecting on the lessons learned from predecessors Jim Brady, Larry Speakes, and Marlin Fitzwater.
articles.body:
The U.S. has just watched the shortest press secretary tenure in its history: five days. Soon, someone new will stand at that podium, stepping into one of the hardest jobs in American public life — and a workplace unlike any other, because the room is named for a predecessor who nearly died doing it: the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room.

Jim Brady was a man I knew and loved. I served eight years in the Reagan White House press office. Three men held that podium in my time there, and each taught me something every press secretary needs.

Brady taught me that the press is not the enemy — it is the instrument. He held the job only ten weeks before a bullet meant for President Reagan changed his life forever, but his influence outlasted everyone’s. He was quick, funny, and utterly without pretense. The reporters who sparred with him adored him, because he understood that the briefing room is where the government explains itself to the governed, and the people asking the questions are how the explaining gets done. You can joust with the press all day; Brady did, happily. You cannot despise them without despising the arrangement itself.

A detail of history: after the shooting, President Reagan never gave Brady’s title away. For nearly eight years, Larry Speakes and then Marlin Fitzwater did the job under other titles, because “press secretary” belonged to Brady until the day the administration ended. That was loyalty — and a lesson: The job is bigger than its occupant.

Larry Speakes taught me the grind. He took the podium on the worst afternoon of the Reagan presidency — March 30, 1981, with the president in surgery and the world demanding answers — then did it for six more years. From Speakes I learned that the briefing is won in the hours before it: the morning papers, the overnight cables, the calls to every corner of the building to find out what was true before someone asked. The podium punishes the unprepared, and no amount of charm survives a guess.

Fitzwater taught me that all you have is your credibility — and that it is spent in a single transaction. He served two presidents of very different temperaments, and the press corps trusted him through both, for one reason: He never lied to them. When he couldn’t say, he said he couldn’t say. The result was that the president’s most loyal defender was also the man reporters believed — which is precisely what made his defense worth anything. A press secretary who will say anything is, professionally speaking, mute.

Here is the structural truth nobody explains on the first day: the job serves three masters. The president, who deserves a vigorous advocate. The press, who are owed straight answers on behalf of their readers. And the public, who own the presidency and are the actual audience for every word said from that podium. The three pull in different directions daily — and the only thing that lets one person serve all three is credibility. Your believability is not your asset; it is the president’s. Spend it never.

So, here is some counsel across the generations for the next press secretary, offered with genuine goodwill. Brief often — the room exists to be used. Prepare like Speakes; the questions are not the test, the facts are.

Never guess, and when you’re wrong, correct fast and plainly. Expect to learn more from the reporters than they learn from you — the good ones have covered that building longer than most of us worked in it; that’s how every press secretary starts. Be the president’s supporter — that is the job — but a supporter is not a sycophant, and the difference is the whole value of the role: an echo persuades no one, while an advocate who is believed is worth divisions. And this, from one communicator to another: Many Americans don’t love the press, and that’s fine. But never be rude to reporters on camera as a performance — contempt manufactured for the clip, to gain favor with anyone, demeans the room, and the room remembers. So does the country.

One more thing about the name on the door. Brady gave the job his body and never got to do it at full strength. The room was named to honor what he represented: the belief that the presidency explains itself — cheerfully, combatively, honestly — to a free press, because the presidency belongs to the public. I would offer this standard to any press secretary of any party, word for word, and I have no doubt Brady would too. The podium is not a shield and not a weapon. It is a promise.

To whoever takes the podium next: Welcome to the hardest job in the building. Good luck. The name on the room will be watching. It is a friendly gaze — and an exacting one.

Mark Weinberg, founder of the executive communications consultancy Ethos, served in the Reagan White House press office for eight years and later as a speechwriter for President Reagan. He is the author of the bestselling book “Movie Nights with the Reagans.” .

articles.title: Trump announces plans to renovate D.C. golf course amid legal battle
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced Sunday that the administration has developed a plan to redevelop a golf course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Sunday that the administration has developed a plan to redevelop the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle over his renovation plans. Trump said that the Interior Department worked with golf course architect Tom Fazio to develop “a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.” “When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said in the post. He said that the renovations would begin on Nov. 15 and take about 15 months. The proposed renovation, though, has already been challenged in court by a preservation group and two D.C. residents. Last week, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes forbade the administration from cutting down more trees at the course through Oct. 26. The administration had cut down hundreds of trees from the course, causing Reyes to hit back, saying she was “furious.” “I was hearing from everyone on plaintiffs’ side this was going to happen. I said repeatedly, ‘No, I trust the government.’ I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” Reyes responded at the time. She also said that incident “cost the government all of its credibility.” Reyes said that the administration must provide her and the plaintiffs three business days’ written advance notice before making any “irreparable modification” to the golf course. The judge previously rejected the plaintiffs’ request for a restraining order because lawyers for the Trump administration said they would provide ample notice of large-scale work. National Park Service officials told Reyes last week that they were aware of no formal plan to renovate East Potomac beyond what they saw from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Trump’s previous social media posts. On Friday, the administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that her “histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial.” The judge will hold a hearing Monday in which she has called on the acting director of the National Park Service and the Interior Department’s chief of staff to testify under oath. In Sunday’s Truth Social post, Trump said that the “current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect.” The golf course renovation is the latest in a string of major changes the president has tried to make to the D.C. landscape. He is continuing to build the White House ballroom and has pushed forward on plans to build a “triumphal arch.” His handpicked Kennedy Center board also voted to close the renowned arts center for renovations, and the administration moved to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, though the lining ended up peeling.

articles.title: Cong seeks Left backing for graduate MLC polls
articles.summary: Congress seeks CPI, CPM and TJS support for Telangana graduates’ MLC polls; Left weighs joint candidate, creating uncertainty for Congress strategy.
articles.body: Hyderabad: After backing an alliance against the CPI-affiliated union in the recently held TGSRTC recognised union elections, Congress has now turned to the Left parties, seeking their support in the upcoming elections to the two graduates’ MLC constituencies.Congress has fielded Sama Rammohan Reddy from the Mahbubnagar-Rangareddy-Hyderabad graduates’ constituency and Ramreddy Sarvotham Reddy from the Nalgonda-Khammam-Warangal graduates’ constituency.Telangana Congress president B Mahesh Kumar Goud said the party is seeking the support of the CPI and CPM as both are partners in the INDIA bloc at the national level.“The CPI is also our alliance partner at the state level. We have also sought the support of Telangana Jana Samithi for the Congress candidates in the two MLC seats. We will seek the support of all like-minded parties and organisations,” he said.However, the Left parties have not yet made up their minds. CPM state secretary John Wesley said the party is also considering fielding a candidate from the Nalgonda-Khammam-Warangal constituency.“There is a proposal to field a candidate supported by the CPM, CPI and eight other Left parties in the state. In the last election, a Left-backed candidate was fielded from the Nalgonda-Khammam-Warangal seat. Now the Congress has sought support. We will discuss the proposal with all Left parties and take a decision soon,” he said.Congress leadership is expected to meet CPI state secretary Kunamneni Sambasiva Rao and other party leaders shortly to formally seek support. Kunamneni said the CPI would take a call after Congress presents its proposal.The lack of a clear commitment from the Left parties, coupled with the possibility of a joint CPI-CPM candidate entering the fray, could complicate Congress’s electoral strategy in the MLC elections, political observers said.The developments come at a time when the ruling party is looking to consolidate support after facing a setback in the recent TGSRTC union elections, making the Left parties’ stand crucial to its prospects in the graduate constituencies.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news.
